summary:
Artemisos is a browser-based astronomy platform developed for NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our project transforms public infrared observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission into an interactive sky viewer, allowing anyone to explore how celestial objects change over time.
Users can search for a region of the sky using celestial coordinates or an object's name, animate observations, explore six infrared detector bands, and compare images from different dates. Artemisos also integrates WISE imagery, exploratory image stacking to provide additional ways to investigate the infrared universe.
Built with Python, Flask, and JavaScript, Artemisos connects to NASA's publicly available astronomical archives and makes complex scientific observations more approachable.
Our goal is to make astronomical exploration more accessible, encourage curiosity, and empower students, citizen scientists, and enthusiasts to identify interesting changes in the sky that could inspire further discoveries.
details:
What is Artemisos?

Artemisos is an interactive web application designed to make NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky observations easier to explore and understand. It addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by allowing users to visualize astronomical images across different observation dates and identify potential changes in position.

Instead of requiring specialized astronomy software or programming experience, Artemisos provides a visual interface that welcomes both beginners and experienced astronomy enthusiasts.

How does it work?

Users can enter Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (DEC) coordinates or search for an astronomical object by name. Artemisos communicates with NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), retrieving available SPHEREx observations from the DR1 and QR3 data collections.

The application organizes these observations into six infrared detector bands and displays them through an interactive timeline. Users can play or pause the sequence, navigate individual observations, zoom in and out, and compare selected images from different dates.

Artemisos also provides several advanced features:

  • 102-channel spectral visualization: Users can explore an infrared pixel spectrum extracted from the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube and export its measurements as CSV.
  • WISE comparison: Images from NASA's Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) can be displayed alongside SPHEREx observations or superimposed using astronomical coordinate alignment.
  • Exploratory spectral measurements: Users can select a position in an image and inspect measurements across available observations.

These tools help users investigate astronomical phenomena while encouraging responsible interpretation of observational data.

Technologies and development

Artemisos was developed using Python, Flask, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The backend connects to NASA's public astronomical archives, processes FITS images, and prepares data for visualization. Scientific Python libraries, including Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib, support astronomical coordinate handling, image processing, and scientific calculations.

The frontend provides interactive controls, responsive layouts, timelines, and visualizations. The application also uses caching and optional processing modes to help balance performance and scientific functionality.

Creativity and innovation

The creative value of Artemisos lies in combining several astronomical comparation methods within a single accessible platform.

Rather than simply displaying static telescope images, it encourages users to investigate how the infrared sky evolves through time and wavelength. Temporal animations, image comparisons, spectral visualization, detector stacking, and observations from different NASA missions work together to provide complementary perspectives of the same region.

Our team considered accessibility, usability, data availability, performance, and the limitations of remote astronomical observations.

Intended impact

We envision Artemisos as a bridge between professional astronomical data and public participation in science.

By making complex infrared observations easier to navigate, the project can support astronomy education, independent exploration, and citizen-science activities. It may help users identify promising candidates for further investigation, including moving objects and variable sources.

Artemisos is an exploratory tool: potential discoveries require independent verification and additional scientific analysis. Our broader goal is to encourage more people to participate in understanding the universe and to demonstrate that meaningful scientific exploration can begin with curiosity and accessible technology.
